prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice atomic clocks that reach a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18 and open new regimes of precision measurement

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the clearest case on the shortlist of a new measurement technique that changes what can be observed. The magic-wavelength idea removes the trap as the limiting systematic, and the strontium and ytterbium clocks built on it reach 10^-18-class stability and accuracy. The result is demonstrated, not proposed. Several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) reproduce it and compare clocks over fibre and free space. It enables relativistic geodesy at the centimetre to millimetre scale, tests of gravitational redshift and of variation of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches, and the pending redefinition of the second. Attribution is clean: Katori proposed and first realised the magic-wavelength lattice clock, and Ye drove the record stability, systematic control and applications. Six of eight opening ballots rank it, four in the top three, with identical credited names, which is unusual agreement on laureates. I think this is the one candidate here where evidence, maturity and attribution all line up.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the optical frequency comb (Hall and Haensch, 2005) and ion-clock and trapped-ion control work (Wineland, 2012) already covered neighbouring ground, so a clock prize can be read as incremental precision improvement rather than a new discovery. Priority is also shared: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, the PTB and NIST groups and the magic-wavelength theory community fall outside a two-name credit, and the pending SI redefinition means the full practical consequence is still ahead. I also note that my own ranking reflects a bias toward measurement tools, which this committee should discount appropriately against discovery-type claims.

responses.point: Johansson ranks lattice clocks only seventh and argues that the optical-comb and ion-clock prizes make this an incremental extension, while placing circuit QED first as a basic-physics demonstration.
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously but disagree on its weight. The 2005 and 2012 prizes rewarded the comb and the control of single ions. They did not reward interrogating thousands of neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice, which moved accuracy and stability down by roughly two orders of magnitude and made a new class of measurements possible. That is a change in what can be measured, not a polish. On circuit QED, I agree it is mature and important, but the 2025 prize already recognised superconducting-circuit physics, and the Wallraff omission makes the credited trio less clean than Katori and Ye.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics first as a true new-tool door-opener and lattice clocks second, with a clean two-laureate configuration.
responses.response: I largely agree with her reading of the clocks and share her criterion that an instrument which opens a door deserves priority. Where I differ is on ordering: aberration correction has the more difficult attribution, since Knut Urban, who led the first TEM corrector demonstration, is outside the credited names, and Olsson raises this herself. For the clocks the credited pair matches the historical record well. If that archival question on B021 can be settled, I would see it as a worthy alternative, but it is not my first choice today.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks lattice clocks first as atomic structure and light-shift theory made into an instrument, with Katori and Ye as a defensible pair.
responses.response: I agree, and her atomic-physics perspective is useful on one point I would stress to others: the magic wavelength is a statement about differential polarizabilities, so the clock's accuracy is set by the atom rather than the trap. Her view that other groups need not be credited is where I am slightly more cautious. A citation should say 'optical lattice clocks' and not imply that Katori and Ye alone built the field, so I would keep the wording generic.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube neutrino astronomy and the EHT first and second as instrument-driven discoveries, and lattice clocks third as precision instrumentation of the highest order.
responses.response: I share his weighting of instrument-driven discovery, but I would qualify his top choice. The diffuse flux is well established, but the source identification rests mainly on IceCube alone, with only a few firm sources (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068), and the allocation among Halzen, Spiering and the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers is contested. Lattice clocks have been reproduced independently in many laboratories at the stated precision. On maturity and reproducibility I think they sit ahead of neutrino astronomy, although I accept that neutrinos have the larger public and astrophysical reach.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first because the Bistritzer-MacDonald mechanism is simple, tested and has opened a whole field.
responses.response: The Bistritzer-MacDonald mechanism is elegant and the reproducibility across groups is impressive, so I keep B022 as an alternative. My reservation is timing: the field dates from 2018, the origin of the superconductivity is not settled, and Cao's role as first author of the decisive papers is outside the three credited names. A prize could be awarded more safely once the mechanism is better understood, whereas the clock result is stable now.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to credit a precision-measurement achievement soon after the 2005 and 2012 prizes on related metrology.
How far the early priority for lattice clocks (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and others, plus the magic-wavelength theory) should affect a two-name credit; I cannot independently verify the full history.
Whether the SI second redefinition should be completed first, or whether the independent reproduction already gives sufficient maturity.
If the committee prefers a discovery-type prize, I have not resolved how to rank the astrophysical candidates (IceCube, EHT) against a measurement-tool prize.
statement.conflict_note: My profile shows no connection to Katori, Ye, JILA or RIKEN, so no conflict is apparent for B036. I do declare a possible conflict for B007 (Rempe, Kimble, Lukin): I work on rare-earth-crystal quantum memories, which sit in that field, and I would recuse myself or defer on that candidate. I also have Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology links to Chalmers, where Goran Johansson is based, which bear on B044 and quantum-technology candidates generally.
